Header:
Date: 2025-09-30
Time: 15:00 PDT (Zoom)
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood SRE); Liam O'Connor (Orion CTO), Sasha Ivanov (Lead ML Eng), Priya Shah (Platform Eng)
Recording ID: ff-20250930-orion-cache-13

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
- Deep dive on prefix/prompt caching strategy: key synthesis, entropy, and safe shared cache for multi-tenant workloads.
- Discussed tradeoffs: global shared cache vs per-tenant namespaces, LRU/LFU/TTL hybrid eviction, consistent hashing for shards, and how quantized model variants affect cache hit stability.
- Action items include bench runs (48h), sharing prefix distribution, and a canary rollout plan for VPC-enabled pilot.

Topics covered:
- key entropy & cardinality measurements
- safe namespacing & collision mitigation
- eviction strategies and cache churn metrics
- impact of quantization on deterministic caching and micro-variation in generation
- batching, throughput vs tail latency considerations
- VPC/on-prem implications for central cache vs local shard caches

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): alright everyone, thank you for joining, I think we have about an hour, appreciate you making time. quick intros?
[00:12] Liam (Orion): Liam here, CTO, quick overview: we're running an in-house assistant across multiple tenants, avg QPS ~120, peak ~900 during business hours, goal is to reduce token cost but keep sub-400ms p50 for chat responses.
[00:30] Maya: perfect, thanks. Diego, want to frame the agenda?
[00:34] Diego (Redwood SE): yeah, we'll look at your prefix distributions Sasha sent, talk key-synthesis options (namespace salt, hashing, prefix truncation), eviction, and then the special case: quantized model variants and whether cache keys remain stable. we'll also cover VPC/on-prem constraints around cache placement.
[00:52] Sasha (Customer ML): quick note, the trace we sent is sampled, there are long-tail prompts that mutate slightly (typos, punctuation). curious how that impacts hit-rate.
[01:10] Diego: good call. small edit/noise in prefix can be huge for exact-match caches—so we need normalization, canonicalization, and maybe fuzzy-prefixing.
[01:22] Priya (Platform): our infra prefers a shared cache to avoid per-tenant capacity waste, but security/legal wants isolation guarantees.
[01:34] Maya: classic tension. we've seen hybrid approaches work: a small per-tenant hot-cache + larger shared global cache with quotas. helps reduce cold-start for new tenants without exploding memory.
[01:48] Liam: can you walk through key format recommendations? we want deterministic keys that don't leak PII.
[01:55] Diego: suggested key = H(salt || tenant_id || prefix_hash || model_variant || quantization_tag). H is siphash/xxhash/sha1 depending on needs. salt ensures no raw prompt text in keys. prefix_hash computed on tokenized prefix (we recommend sub-word tokenization like BPE before hashing).
[02:22] Sasha: tokenization differences between quantized and fp16 models? will tokenization change cached keys?
[02:29] Diego: tokenizers are model-agnostic usually; quantization affects weights not tokenization. but model_variant tag must be part of the key because different model variants can produce divergent continuation given same prefix.
[02:45] Maya: also include sequence length cap for prefix keys; long prefixes truncated to N tokens to keep cardinality manageable. that's a parameter we'll propose.
[03:00] Liam: what's a reasonable N?
[03:02] Diego: depends on workload. from your histogram, 90% of prefixes under 48 tokens. we often choose 64 as a safe upper bound, sometimes 128 for high-context apps. longer increases uniqueness and reduces shared hits.
[03:20] Sasha: hit-rate numbers in our demo cluster were weird—dev saw 78% but production more like 61% after dedupe. why the delta?
[03:30] Diego: a few likely reasons: (1) more diverse user prompts in prod, (2) lack of normalization (casing/punctuation), (3) transient tenant-specific tokens like user ids that need masking, (4) different model variants or A/B buckets.
[03:50] Maya: we recommend a normalization pass: lowercasing optional, strip ephemeral tokens via regex, or replace common user placeholders. but be careful: over-normalization can reduce correctness. usually we provide a canonicalizer lib customers can tune.
[04:10] Priya: on multi-tenant safety, are there risks that shared caches leak info between tenants via hit/no-hit side channels? security wants to be conservative.
[04:20] Diego: yes there are side-channels; shared cache can reveal whether a prefix exists (timing, hit counts). mitigations: per-tenant quotas, per-tenant opaque keys (salted with tenant-specific K), and adding small random jitter to latency metrics in certain cases. full cryptographic isolation needs per-tenant cache shards.
[04:42] Liam: we prefer not to spin up hundreds of tiny caches. can consistent hashing + tenant caps work?
[04:48] Diego: yes, consistent hashing distributes keys to shards; apply tenant weight/cap and local eviction per-shard. plus include an admission policy that rejects global entries if they exceed tenant's memory budget.
[05:05] Sasha: about eviction: LRU vs LFU vs TTL? our workload has bursty repetitiveness followed by dormancy.
[05:13] Diego: for bursty workloads a hybrid works: LFU for long-term popularity, LRU for recency, plus TTL for staleness. We often implement a two-tier: a tiny per-tenant LRU hot cache and a larger LFU global cache.
[05:30] Maya: add metric 'cache-churn-rate' and 'per-tenant cold-starts per minute' to instrument policy effectiveness.
[05:38] Sasha: how do quantized models affect cache correctness? if a quantized variant returns slightly different logits, are cached continuations still valid?
[05:46] Diego: if the model variant is included in key, it's safe in the sense of identical model variant returns identical continuation. but if you switch variants (e.g., fp16 -> int8) and don't invalidate, you risk quality regressions. we recommend model-variant-aware invalidation and staged rollouts.
[06:05] Priya: interesting, so variant tag mandatory. what about cross-variant fallback? e.g., miss on int8, then check fp16?
[06:13] Diego: you can implement fallback but must treat it as a controlled policy: fallback increases latency; also you need to ensure you don't leak that a variant had a hit.
[06:25] Liam: network and VPC concerns: if we run cache in our VPC on-prem, what are tradeoffs?
[06:31] Maya: local cache inside VPC reduces cross-region latency and data egress but increases ops burden. Redwood offers a private cache appliance pattern: deploy a small sharded cluster in VPC with a control plane that is privacy-preserving.
[06:46] Priya: do you have recommended sharding size per region?
[06:49] Diego: rule of thumb: each shard ~64-128GB RAM for high hit-rate, target under 400ms tail. consistent hash 8-16 virtual nodes per physical node for evenness. but we'll model exact numbers in the bench.
[07:05] Sasha: question on key collisions: if we truncate or use short hashes there's a collision risk—how to detect and recover?
[07:13] Diego: use a two-step: store small provenance metadata with each entry (prefix_fingerprint, tenant_id, model_tag). on lookup, verify the fingerprint matches; if mismatch, treat as miss. cheap overhead but prevents silent cross-key pollution.
[07:30] Maya: that also helps audits and debugging. keep metadata size minimal.
[07:36] Liam: said earlier you mentioned 'fuzzy prefixing' —what is that in practice?
[07:40] Diego: instead of exact-match on token sequence, compute n-gram fingerprints or a Bloom filter sketch of recent tokens and allow approximate match if overlap above threshold. good for minor punctuation/typo variance. downside: false positives and increased complexity.
[08:00] Sasha: sounds risky. our quality bar is high, but maybe for non-critical responses we can accept fuzzy hits.
[08:08] Diego: exactly, toggle by route. Redwood supports per-route cache policies so you can enable fuzzy on low-risk routes.
[08:15] Priya: batching: if we increase batch size for GPU util, does that reduce cache benefit?
[08:21] Diego: batching interacts: larger batches increase throughput but can increase first-token latency. cache helps reduce tokens generated so it can reduce overall GPU time. we recommend dynamic batch sizing tied to SLOs and a prioritization queue for cached responses vs cold requests.
[08:40] Maya: also, when cache hit is mostly prefix-based, you can short-circuit expensive kv-fetches by doing local L1 lookup before dispatching to batch queue, reduces tail.
[08:50] Liam: telemetry: what do you want us to send?
[08:52] Diego: per-request: tenant_id (hash), route, prefix_token_count, model_variant, cache_key_present(boolean), cache_hit, latency_ms, shard_id. also aggregated histograms for prefix length and key cardinality.
[09:10] Sasha: any tooling for visualizing key entropy?
[09:13] Diego: we'll share a heatmap tool; Maya will drop an initial entropy heatmap.
[09:18] Maya: yep, heatmap + unique-key-per-minute, churn rate, per-tenant hit-rate.
[09:25] Priya: about privacy audits: if someone requests logs, we need to ensure cached entries don't contain PII. how do you handle that?
[09:33] Diego: we advise masking/normalization pre-hash and not storing raw prompts in cache. store only small fingerprint + synthetic provenance. when higher compliance needed, deploy per-tenant cache in customer VPC and use HSM-backed salt.
[09:47] Liam: rolling update plan for cache invalidation during model upgrades?
[09:50] Diego: a canary: keep both variants in parallel, tag keys with variant, and gradually switch routing. when promoting new variant, a background job can pre-warm cache by replaying popular prefixes. and set aggressive TTLs during rollout to limit stale hits.
[10:10] Sasha: we'd like to try pre-warm. what's the cost implication?
[10:14] Maya: pre-warm is traffic-driven; it's basically issuing controlled requests. cost is compute + small token usage; often worth it to avoid cold-start tail. Diego will estimate from your trace.
[10:25] Liam: ok what's the proposed canary for us?
[10:28] Diego: 48h bench with your 7-day sample, run three variants: fp16 baseline, int8 quantized, and int8 + small kernel optimizations. measure per-route hit-rate, p50/p95 latency, and cache-churn.
[10:42] Maya: and concurrently we'll generate prefix-entropy heatmap for the 7-day window.
[10:47] Priya: any gotchas for on-prem proxies? we have an L7 proxy that does TLS termination.
[10:53] Diego: ensure the proxy preserves the hashed tenant_id header (not the raw). avoid re-writing payloads. if the proxy times out shorter than model latency you can get partial responses — need alignment of timeouts.
[11:05] Liam: can we give Redwood access to a staging VPC for benching?
[11:08] Priya: security may allow short-term peering with limited IPs and timebox. I'll check.
[11:12] Maya: perfect. we'll need an endpoint and some sample creds. we'll provide an ingestion script to replay traces.
[11:18] Sasha: quick nit: what hash function is fastest? we saw xxhash in our microbench.
[11:22] Diego: xxhash or siphash; xxhash fastest but not keyed; siphash has better DoS resistance. choice depends on threat model. we default to keyed siphash for tenant-safety, fallback to xxhash in low-risk internal caches.
[11:36] Priya: what about storage format, Redis vs custom LSM?
[11:40] Diego: Redis is easy and ubiquitous but doesn't scale for multi-GB per-node without clustering complexity. We use a custom in-memory slab with optional on-disk backing in our private offering; for private deploys we can recommend memory-optimized Redis clusters or Rocksdb-based caches depending on LRU semantics needed.
[11:58] Liam: anything else on metrics or operational runbooks?
[12:00] Diego: alert on sudden drop in global hit-rate, % of tenant misses above threshold, cache-churn spike, and tail latency. have an automated rollback to bypass cache for a short window if corruption suspected.
[12:15] Maya: recap and next steps: Diego runs bench, Maya shares heatmap & docs, Sasha uploads sanitized traces, Priya confirms VPC peering. we'll meet for canary kickoff.
[12:28] Liam: sounds good. a few smaller clarifications might follow via email.
[12:32] Maya: great, thanks everyone. end of call.

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker overlap; some words auto-corrected (e.g., "prefex" -> "prefix"), timestamps approximate.
